instruction: Explain the concept of discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.
response: The DCF is used to value assets that have no market price and therefore cannot be sold for their full intrinsic value at any point in time. The basic idea behind this approach is that you can calculate how much money an asset will generate over its lifetime if it were to continue operating as planned without being replaced or depreciated. This calculation would then serve as your estimate of what the future values of those assets might be worth today.  In other words: If I could sell my house now for $100K, but it was still fully depreciating, wouldn't that make me more valuable than someone who bought it five years ago when it had only been half-depreciated? Yes! But since we're talking about real-world investments here - not just hypothetical scenarios - there's some additional considerations involved. For example, let's say that instead of selling the house right away, you decide to keep it until retirement so that you don't lose out on appreciation during inflationary periods. Then you'd need to factor in the fact that the house may appreciate even further after retirement due to rising interest rates. instruction: A company revenue increased by 20% from last year to $120 million. What was the revenue last year?
response: The formula for calculating growth is: Growth = (Current Value - Previous Value) / Previous Value * 100 % The current value of your answer should be $80M because you have already added in inflation when computing this number.

instruction: Explain why a company can have increasing revenue but decreasing net profit.
response: "Revenue is the money that you make from selling something or providing services to customers.  Net Profit (or Gross Profit) is what remains after all expenses and taxes were paid on your income before any profits were made. So if you're making more than zero in Revenue then there must be some amount of Expenses which will reduce it below Zero. If this number was less than zero - meaning that you had negative Income at least once during the period - then you would not have been able to cover those costs with the additional revenues generated so far."

instruction: Does a high price-to-earnings ratio always mean that a stock is overvalued? Explain.
response: "An ""over-valued"" stock means the share prices of all stocks in an industry or sector have increased significantly compared to their historical average and/or relative to other companies' shares.  This can be caused by many things: A company's earnings per share (EPS) has gone up dramatically; The market believes there will be more profits from this business going forward; There was some news about something bad happening with the company but it hasn't happened yet - so they're not worried anymore; Other factors such as changes in regulations could also cause EPS to go up."

instruction: Explain how rising interest rates usually affect stock markets.
response: "Interest rate hikes have the effect of making borrowing more expensive and therefore reducing investment in fixed income securities such as bonds (which is why they tend to rise).  This makes it less attractive for investors to hold these types of investments so their prices fall. The effects on stocks can be different depending on what type of bond you're talking about: In general, if there's an increase in demand from investors who want to invest money into something that pays out regular dividends or has some other special features then this will make those things worth buying because people think they'll get back their original cost plus any extra returns over time. If however, there isn't enough demand for them at all - meaning no one wants to buy them - then even though they might pay higher prices now than before due to inflation, nobody would ever actually take advantage of the price difference anyway since everyone else already owns them. So when we talk about ""interest"" here, I'm assuming you mean annualized interest payments rather than just nominal ones like monthly or quarterly."

instruction: A company reports strong sales growth but negative operating cash flow for several years. What might this indicate?
response: "First of all you need to understand that the ""negative"" is not necessarily bad.  It's just an indication that your business isn't making enough money in order to cover its expenses and pay off debt (or at least keep up with it). The fact that they have so many losses doesn't mean anything about their future prospects or how well they will do going forward. They may be able to make more profit if they improve efficiency, reduce costs, increase revenue, etc., without having to borrow additional funds."

instruction: Explain the difference between revenue, profit, and cash flow.
response: Revenue is what you get from selling something or providing services to customers.  It's usually expressed as an amount of money in your pocket (or bank account). Profit is how much more than expenses you have left after paying all costs for producing goods/services that were sold. This can be calculated using net income: Net Income = Revenue - Expenses If there was no cost associated with production, then this would just equal the revenue. However, if some additional costs had been incurred during production, such as rent on equipment used to produce products, depreciation on machinery, etc., then we'd need to subtract those amounts from our total revenues before calculating profits. instruction: An investment of $10,000 earns a 5% annual compound return. Approximately how much will it become after 10 years?
response: The formula for the future value is: FV = P(1 + r)^n Where:   -FV is Future Value (the amount that you want to have in your account at some point in time) -P is Principal Amount (how much money you already have in your bank or other savings account right now) -r is Rate of Return (in decimal form; i.e., if you earn 2%, then r=0.02) -n is Number of Periods (or Years). In this case we know all three values and need only one more number to solve our problem. The answer should be close enough to what you're looking for so I'll just plug in numbers from memory. So let's say you start with $10,000 today and invest it into an account earning 3%. After 10 years there would be approximately $46,978 left over on top of whatever interest was earned during those ten years.

instruction: Explain why diversification can reduce investment risk.
response: Diversifying your investments is one way to spread out the risks of investing in different types and levels of assets (stocks vs bonds, real estate etc).  The idea behind this strategy is that you will not lose all or most of what you have invested if something goes wrong with any particular asset class. Diversified portfolios tend to be more stable than those which invest only in single asset classes because they contain many different kinds of securities. For example, stocks may perform well but also suffer from volatility; bond funds might do better but still face some level of interest rate risk; mutual fund managers who specialize in certain sectors such as technology could make good money on their own returns while losing less when things go south for other sectors. A diversified portfolio would therefore provide an additional layer of protection against losses due to market fluctuations across various asset categories. However, it's important to note that there are two main reasons why diversification does not completely eliminate risk: First, even though individual stock prices fluctuate around average values over time, overall stock markets generally move up and down together. This means that although individual companies' performance varies widely between periods, large changes in company valuations don't happen very often. instruction: Can any investment strategy guarantee profits under all market conditions? Explain.
response: "An investor can make money in the stock market if they have an understanding of how to invest and what not to do with their investments.  The key is that you understand your risk tolerance (how much loss you're willing to accept) and your time horizon (what's it going to take for you to get back some or all of your initial capital). If you don't know enough about investing, then there will be no guarantees at all."

instruction: Explain the relationship between inflation and purchasing power.
response: "Inflation is an increase in prices of goods and services over time.  In general terms it means that your money will lose value as you use more of it to buy things (or not). The price level refers to how much one unit of currency can be bought with other units of currency at any given point in time. So if I have $100 today, then my purchase power would be limited only by what I could get for this amount using whatever medium of exchange exists right now - paper notes or coins, cash on hand etc. If we assume that all currencies exist forever, then there's no limit to how many times you might need to spend out of something worth just $100. But let's say that instead of having $100, you had $250. Then when you spent some of that away, you'd still owe someone else $75 because they couldn't give you back another $250. And so even though you've got two dollars left, you're actually paying less than half of what you originally owed them."

instruction: Why do banks need to maintain capital adequacy ratios?
response: "Capital is the money that banks have put aside as an insurance policy against losses in their assets (such as loans).  The more you can deposit with your bank and keep it safe from loss - the better off they will be when there's something wrong with them. Banks don't want to lose all of this money if things go south; so they must make sure that they're not losing too much money on each loan or other asset. This means keeping some portion of their balance sheet as ""capital"". In theory, these funds should never run out because we know how long people take to pay back our debts: just like you'd expect us to get paid for every dollar we owe! instruction: Explain the difference between stocks and bonds.
response: "Stocks: A stock is an investment in which you own a share of ownership or interest in something (such as a company).  The value of your shares can fluctuate based on how well that company does financially over time. Bonds: Bond refers to any debt instrument issued by a government or other entity with some form of obligation for repayment at specified dates. In general terms, it's anything where there is money involved - whether its cash flow from business operations, dividends paid out to shareholders, etc."

instruction: A company's debt increases significantly while its revenue remains unchanged. What risks might this create?
response: "First of all you need to understand that the term ""debt"" is not always bad for your business.  If it was then everyone would be doing it and no one could make money from it. The problem with debt in general is that if there isn't enough cash flow coming into the business (or even just some) they will have trouble paying their debts. So when I say debt can increase risk here means: When you look at how much debt does each firm have, what percentage of total revenues do these firms get paid back on over time, etc., you'll see that most companies don't pay off their loans as quickly or as well as they should."

instruction: Explain how financial statements help investors evaluate a company.
response: Financial Statements: A Financial Statement is an account of the assets and liabilities (the money that you have) as well as your income for a particular period of time.  The most common types of financial statement include Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow Statement etc. These accounts will tell us what happened to our business in one year or over several years. For example if we look at the balance sheet it shows all the cash balances on hand plus any loans outstanding minus anything paid off with interest - this tells us whether we had enough cash reserves to cover our debts when they were due. If we also looked at the income statement then we would know exactly how much profit was made during the same period. This information can be used to make decisions about investing in the stock market because it gives us insight into past performance which helps predict future results.

instruction: Why can past stock performance not guarantee future returns?
response: "Stock prices fluctuate over time because of many factors: 1) The company's financials (profitability and cash flow). If the company is profitable but has negative cash flows or losses it will have lower price than if it was making money. 2) Market sentiment about the company. People who think that the company should be bought would buy more shares at higher prices while people who don't like what they see in their portfolio might sell off some to get out of it. This creates an inverse relationship between how much you want to invest now vs. how much you'll actually end up investing later on. 3) Investor expectations for the company. Investors expect companies with high growth rates to grow faster than average; investors also expect companies with low risk to do so as well. So when there isn't enough information available regarding these things then we cannot predict whether something good will happen or bad will happen."

instruction: Explain the difference between active investing and passive investing.
response: "Active Investing is when you try to make money off of your own research on stocks or other investments. Passive Investing is where an investment manager takes care of all aspects of running their portfolio (buying shares, selling them at market prices) for you."

instruction: A company has high profits but low cash reserves. Explain why this situation may happen.
response: "First of all you need to understand that the word ""profit"" is not always positive and it can be negative as well.  The profit statement shows how much money was made in one period (usually quarter or year). If your business makes more than expected then its profitable; if less than expected then its unprofitable.   Now lets look at what happens when there's no cash flow from sales: When there isn't any revenue for the month, we have zero net income! This means that our total assets will increase while liabilities decrease because we owe nothing now. So even though we make $10K last month, we still don't have anything left over after paying off debt. In fact, since we didn't pay off our debts yet, we're actually worse off financially than before - we've lost some value due to inflation which could easily amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars per year. That said, I think most companies would rather go bankrupt than lose their customers forever."

instruction: Explain why Bitcoin or other cryptocurrencies have highly volatile prices.
response: "Bitcoin is not the only cryptocurrency that has high volatility and low liquidity (i.e.: it's hard to buy/ sell).  The reason for this is because of its ""decentralized"" nature: unlike central banks which can control monetary policy through their money supply, all transactions in bitcoin happen on an open network where there isn't any single point of authority controlling them. This means that if you want to make sure your transaction gets processed quickly enough so as to be able to get paid back later - then you need to do something about how fast they're processing these transactions! In order to keep up with demand, miners will often spend more time waiting than needed until some block is mined before being rewarded with new bitcoins. So while mining costs may seem like a small price to pay when compared to the potential reward from getting bitcoins, it does add up over time. As such, many people who invest in BTC tend to wait longer between trades since they know that once they've made a trade, they'll probably never see another one again."

instruction: What factors should investors consider before investing in a company?
response: "First of all you need to understand the business model and how it works.  If your investment is into an online game or software development then there's no question that this will be very volatile as these companies can go bankrupt at any time without warning. The other thing I would look for when making decisions about investments is whether they have good management (which means someone who knows what he/she is doing) and if so - does their management know what they're doing well enough to make them happy with his/her decision-making process? This may not always be true but it could help keep some people from getting too invested in one particular stock."
